title: Weight-Loss Drug Prescriptions for US Children Under 12 Surge 310-Fold Since 2019
excerpt: A new NYU Langone study finds 20,282 children ages 8 to 11 received GLP-1 drugs like Wegovy and Zepbound, with access disparities already emerging along income lines.
body:
• GLP-1 weight-loss drug prescriptions for US children ages 8 to 11 rose 310-fold between 2019 and June 2026, according to a new study in the journal Pediatrics.
  • A total of 20,282 children under 12 received drugs like Wegovy, Saxenda, or Zepbound during the study period — still a small fraction of the estimated 3.3 million eligible children.
  • Nearly 94 percent of children prescribed GLP-1s had severe obesity, and 65 percent had at least one related condition such as high cholesterol or sleep apnea.
  • Children in higher-income communities were 55 percent more likely to receive prescriptions, raising concerns about access disparities.

The Numbers Behind the Surge

Prescriptions for GLP-1 weight-loss drugs among US children under 12 have increased more than 300-fold since 2019, according to a study published September 4 in the journal Pediatrics. Led by researchers at NYU Langone Health, the study analyzed data from more than 3.5 million children ages 8 to 11 with obesity but without diabetes.

The proportion of children in this age group prescribed glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists rose from 0.03 percent in 2019 to 9.3 percent as of June 2026. In total, 20,282 children received GLP-1 drugs during the 7.5-year study period — most commonly Novo Nordisk's Wegovy, followed by Novo's Saxenda and Eli Lilly's Zepbound, according to Reuters.

Off-Label but Not Without Guardrails

No GLP-1 medication is currently FDA-approved for use in children under 12. However, clinical guidelines from the American Academy of Pediatrics allow the medications to be prescribed for obesity in children as young as eight in certain cases, forming the basis for the off-label use documented in the study.

The vast majority of children prescribed GLP-1s were not borderline cases. Nearly 94 percent had severe obesity, meaning their BMI was substantially higher than almost all other children of the same age and sex. About 65 percent had at least one obesity-related complication, including high cholesterol, high blood pressure, or sleep apnea. A quarter were prediabetic, according to the NYU Langone research.

"The concern isn't that more children are being treated; rather, it's that so many need to be, so many already have complications of obesity."

— Dr. Babak Orandi, NYU Langone Health

Access Gaps Are Already Emerging

The study revealed early signs of an equity divide. Children living in upper-income communities were 55 percent more likely to be prescribed GLP-1 medications than those in lower-income areas, suggesting that access to these treatments is already uneven. Girls were also more likely than boys to receive prescriptions.

"Physicians and health policymakers alike have a responsibility to ensure that these valuable and sometimes costly treatments become available to more than those who have access to health insurance and can afford to visit pediatric clinics," said Allan Massie, co-author of the study and associate professor of surgery at NYU Grossman School of Medicine.

Long-Term Safety Still Unknown

The rapid uptake comes with a significant caveat: long-term safety data for GLP-1 use in young children remains limited. Lead investigator Dr. Babak Orandi said ongoing monitoring is essential to ensure the drugs remain safe and effective in this age group. Clinical trials involving GLP-1 medications in children as young as six with obesity are already underway, which will help inform physicians, policymakers, and parents, according to MedicalXpress.

The researchers used Epic Cosmos, a national dataset of electronic health records covering more than 300 million American patients across 2,067 hospitals and 47,100 health clinics.

What Parents Should Know

While the 310-fold increase sounds alarming, the absolute numbers remain small. Against an estimated 3.3 million children ages 8 to 11 with obesity in the US, the 20,282 who received GLP-1 prescriptions represent a tiny fraction. The study suggests physicians are prescribing cautiously and primarily to children with the most severe cases and existing complications.

For Indian-American parents, the study underscores a broader public health reality: childhood obesity rates in the US continue to climb, and medical interventions are increasingly part of the conversation alongside diet and lifestyle changes. The emerging access gap also raises questions about whether South Asian communities, which face elevated metabolic risks, have equitable access to these treatments when needed.
